newsitem.title: RUSSIA: CIS fails to live up to post-Soviet vision - Kuchma.
newsitem.headline: CIS fails to live up to post-Soviet vision - Kuchma.

text.p: More than five years on, the Commonwealth of Independent States is a long way from becoming a post-Soviet equivalent of the European Union and its future looks bleak, Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma said on Thursday.
In Moscow on the eve of a summit of CIS leaders, Kuchma said the body remained vague and divided into blocs, hampering rather than fostering closer integration among its 12 members.

He held out little hope that the summit would bring a breakthrough, although he said Ukraine understood that it had to live with Russia and did not reject the idea of a loose union with other former Soviet republics.
"I think that today not a single representative of the countries in the Commonwealth is satisfied by the results of its activities, because there aren't any," Kuchma said.
"The Commonwealth is quite amorphous, not that which had been envisaged at the very beginning," he told a news conference. "We should aim for the European type."
Ukraine is among the most sceptical members of the CIS, which is made up of all the former Soviet republics except the three Baltic states and was founded after the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991.

He and other sceptics feel that Moscow, which holds a strong regional card in the form of energy supplies, is too dominant in the organisation, designed to foster trade between the 12 struggling post-communist economies.
"When each country has certain privileges within the Commonwealth I think it doesn't foster the mood of togetherness," he said.
"Its future depends on Russia. The key is in Moscow. There's no point looking for the answer to this question in the other capitals," he said.
Kuchma said the blocs included Russia and Belarus, which are discussing possible unification, and Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, which have formed a customs union.

That union, one of the Commonwealth's few high-profile economic deals, has been fraught with problems and is in danger of falling apart. Kazakhstan said last week it was thinking of leaving it because it did not work.
Ukraine's own relations with Russia are also under strain and Kuchma was cautious about his meeting with Yeltsin, which follows a long hiatus due to the Kremlin leader's ill health.
Yeltsin has failed to carry out promises to visit Kiev to sign a friendship treaty.
"We have declared more than once that the main problems have been resolved, that tomorrow or the day after the Russian president will visit Kiev. It's always tomorrow, tomorrow, tomorrow," he said.
But, in an appeal for compromise, he added: "I don't want to sound as if I am making ultimatums."
The main sticking point in Ukrainian-Russian relations is control over Sevastopol on the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, the port where the former Soviet Black Sea fleet is based.
The row, which has held up the signing of a broad bilateral treaty, centres on the demand by some politicians in Moscow for Sevastopol to be declared a Russian town, something Ukraine has ruled out.
